data.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care_

**Class:** Modern moist wound-healing dressings

## Mechanism of action
- Maintain a moist wound environment → faster epithelialisation, autolytic debridement, less pain; choice depends on exudate amount and wound depth

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Films (polyurethane, semi-permeable): clean superficial wounds, donor sites, IV sites — no absorption
- Hydrocolloids: light–moderate exudate, autolytic debridement of sloughy wounds, pressure ulcers (occlusive; not for infected wounds)
- Hydrogels: dry/necrotic wounds — donate moisture, rehydrate eschar; burns, radiation dermatitis
- Alginates (calcium alginate from seaweed): heavily exuding and bleeding wounds (haemostatic, forms gel); cavities
- Foams: moderate–heavy exudate, around tubes, under compression
- Others: silver/iodine antimicrobial dressings, honey, activated charcoal (odour), paraffin tulle (non-adherent), skin substitutes (Apligraf), negative pressure wound therapy

## Dose & formulations
- Change according to exudate (hydrocolloids every 3–7 days; alginates/foams when saturated)

## Adverse effects
- Maceration of surrounding skin, allergy to adhesives (colophony), hydrocolloid odour/residue mistaken for infection

## Contraindications
- Occlusive dressings on infected wounds (hydrocolloids); dry wounds for alginates

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not applicable.

## Viva points
- Match the dressing to the exudate: dry → hydrogel; heavy → alginate/foam
- Hydrocolloid gel and odour can mimic infection

_Sources: Khopkar ch.32 (Wound care products — films, hydrocolloids, hydrogels, alginates, foams, artificial skin substitutes); Wolverton 4e ch.54. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
